writing.explanation:
For n=3, append '(' first whenever openings remain. Only close an unmatched opening. The five valid strings are emitted in lexicographic order; n=0 has one valid empty construction, not a failed search.

The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: Return valid sequences for three pairs in lexicographic order. The visible fixture is `n=3` and its example result is `((()));(()());(())();()(());()()()`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

A problem is a good match for Valid Parentheses Generation when it asks for balanced sequence construction. Here the concrete task is: Return valid sequences for three pairs in lexicographic order. The visible input `n=3` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Use pruning when partial choices can already be ruled out. Meet-in-the-middle instead trades two exhaustive half-enumerations for a smaller search space. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Add an open symbol while available and a close only when it cannot exceed opens used. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? Most patterns here explore a decision tree; meet-in-the-middle instead enumerates two halves and combines them. Define the partial choice or subset summary that the pattern retains. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(Catalan(n)*n) time · O(n) depth; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `((()));(()());(())();()(());()()()` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Test no solution, one solution, duplicate inputs, and the order in which candidates are tried if output order is observable. For recursive search, push a choice, recurse, then undo it; for meet-in-the-middle, collect each half before matching them. In Rust, clone a path only when storing a completed answer. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output.
